body: It is a quarter past two on a Sunday afternoon and the food is going cold. The grandmother has been praying over it for some time. She began with the food, moved on to the man who grew it, and is currently somewhere in the middle of an aunt in another country whose knee has been bad since the spring. Nobody at the table is startled. A boy of nine has his eyes open and is watching a skin form on the gravy, and he has heard this prayer, or one very like it, several hundred times. When she finishes, everybody says amen at slightly different moments and the plates start moving.

Nobody in that room believed a lesson was under way, least of all the boy, who was thinking about the gravy. But something had been taught, and it was not the content of the prayer. It was that this is a thing adults do out loud.

There are cultures in which prayer is a private act performed silently, and cultures in which it is ordinary to hear it. A grandmother praying at length over a meal. Somebody praying at a doorway before a journey. A whole room praying at once, audibly, not in unison.

The audible habit is usually treated as informal by people from the other tradition, or as insufficiently reverent, or simply as noise. It is worth defending, and the argument is practical rather than sentimental. Prayer is a register of speech, and almost nobody has ever learned a register from instruction. Registers are picked up the way a child picks up any way of talking — by standing about while competent speakers use it imperfectly, for years, with nobody announcing anything. A child raised where prayer is silent has been told that adults pray. A child raised where it is audible has heard what praying sounds like, which is a different piece of information entirely.

The dial runs from HM 300.30 to HM 398.70 and carries 121 stations across 29 languages. Prayer holds frequencies of its own rather than a slot on somebody else’s — among them HM 351.10, Jubilee Prayers in Portuguese, which is assigned and in build and not yet on air.

Building it that way costs more than the alternative. Translating a prayer is cheap and quick; hosting one is neither, because cadence cannot be commissioned. The rhythm of how a people prays out loud belongs to the people who do it, and the only way onto a transmitter is to find somebody who already has it and give them the hour. That does not scale, which is why the prayer band fills one frequency at a time. It is done anyway for a plain reason. A child who has heard adults pray out loud, badly, at the kitchen table, has been given something no curriculum supplies.

That inheritance is being quietly spent, usually for good motives. Somewhere along the way the instruction about going into your room and shutting the door got read as a rule against ever being heard, when what it was aimed at was performance before an audience assembled for the purpose. Collapsing those two has produced a generation of believing adults who will speak in front of their children about money, illness and death, and will not pray in front of them. The children draw the obvious conclusion, which is that this belongs with the things adults do not say out loud.

The band is arranged so that the register a listener needs can be found by feel. The prayer frequencies sit together in their own stretch rather than scattered through the music. The international stations are hosted in their languages rather than dubbed into them, which is why a Portuguese prayer hour sounds like Portuguese prayer and not like an English one wearing a coat. Learn roughly where things sit and you can move about the dial without looking, which is the one skill a real band teaches and a search box never can.
None of which is an argument against praying quietly. It is an argument about what a household loses when quiet is its only setting.

Be fair to the silent tradition first, because it does real work. Written prayer carries precision across centuries, and a collect sanded down by four hundred years of use will say in one sentence what most of us cannot manage in ten. Silence protects the shy and stops prayer turning into a competition. Anybody who has sat through a meeting where people prayed at each other through God knows what it is guarding against. But a prayer book cannot be overheard going wrong. It has been finished for centuries. Nothing in it hesitates, doubles back, or runs out of words halfway through and keeps going regardless — and that is precisely the part a child needs to hear.
Nobody has ever learned a language they were never allowed to hear.

A woman of twenty-six is standing at the foot of a hospital bed at about nine in the evening with her coat still on. Her uncle is asleep, or nearly. An aunt looks across and says, you went to church, you do it — because she is the one who went, for about three years, a while ago now. She has never prayed out loud in her life. She starts, and it is bad. She says the word Lord four times in the first sentence, thanks God for something that has not happened yet, loses the thread, stands there in the middle of it, and finishes anyway. Nobody remarks on how it went. The aunt squeezes her arm on the way out. In the lift she notices, with some irritation, that the rhythm she had been using was her grandmother’s.
She was never taught that and she could not do it well. What she had was a shape, put into her at a table on Sundays by somebody with no idea she was doing it. Under pressure the shape was there.

It should be said plainly that the audible habit goes wrong often, and not trivially. Prayer out loud can turn into an address to the room. It can become a way of telling somebody off with God as the intermediary, or of announcing how much of the Bible one has by heart, or of holding a table hostage while the food goes cold. Children have been bored rigid by it, adults humiliated by it. Anybody defending the practice who pretends otherwise has not been in enough kitchens.

But notice which part of that is the actual fault. Not the volume, not the length, and certainly not the clumsiness. What goes wrong is an audience being played to. Take the audience away and the clumsiness turns out to be the useful part, because a prayer that stumbles is the only kind that teaches a listening child that fluency was never the entry requirement. A polished prayer, delivered smoothly, teaches the opposite very efficiently: that this is a skill, that other people have it, and that you had better not attempt it until you do.

So the habit is worth keeping, and worth restarting in households that have mislaid it. Not as a performance, and not as family devotions with a set hour and a printed order, which is a heavier thing altogether and one most families abandon by the third week. Simply out loud, in front of each other, in whatever state the words arrive in. The whole of it is that the children in the room hear the language used by people who are not good at it.
All of which is theory until something is actually playing. So here is the part that is not theory.

Four kinds of programming sit on this dial and it helps to know they are there before you start turning. Most of the band is music — praise and worship, contemporary, country, gospel, hymns and a great deal besides. There is teaching and prayer, where the Word is opened, explained and prayed through rather than sung. There is family programming, safe to have on in a room with children in it. And there are the international frequencies, hosted in their own languages rather than translated into them afterwards. No menu, no queue to assemble, no decision to make before anything begins.

If you want somewhere to start, start at HM 321.90 — Brasil Inspire. It is on air, it is in Portuguese, and it is the closest thing on the dial to the room this article opened in. Brazilian worship is congregational by instinct: it assumes a building full of people who are all going to be audible, and it does not tidy that away in the mix. If Portuguese is your household language, or your grandmother’s, that is reason enough. If it is not, put it on for a week regardless: what comes out of the speaker is a room that was never taught to be quiet about this.

There is nothing to install. No app, no download and no card. Open kJubilee.com on whatever phone or laptop is nearest and press play — it is built deliberately for inexpensive phones and thin connections, so it starts on the hardware people actually have. If you would like it closer to hand, add the page to your home screen and it opens like anything else on it. And do make yourself an account while you are there. It keeps your favourites with you across every Jubilee site, and it is how this band learns which frequencies people reach for, which is how the next one gets built and in which language.

So take this as an invitation rather than a case. You are not being asked to agree with any of it, and you are certainly not being asked to institute anything. Put HM 321.90 on this Sunday while the food is being got ready, leave it running through the meal, and then, when the plates are down, say the words yourself instead of leaving them to the radio. Do it badly. Somebody at that table is nine and is not listening, and that has never once been the point.
